intro: Many Hindu families tell stories at home. Two favorites are about Krishna and Ganesha. Children hear them at festivals and at bedtime.
Many Hindus honor Krishna and Ganesha as forms of God. You will hear their stories. You will hear how families celebrate them.
By the end, you can retell two stories. You can name two festivals. You can say what each story helps children think about.
bigQuestion: What do the stories families tell help children learn?

timeline.t: Little Krishna grows up in a cowherd village
Krishna sneaks butter and shares it with friends
A great storm comes to the village
Krishna lifts Govardhan Hill to keep everyone dry
Ganesha and Kartikeya start a race around the world
Kartikeya flies away on his peacock
Ganesha walks around his parents and says they are his world
Families tell these stories at Janmashtami and Ganesh Chaturthi

write.prompt: Draw and tell. Pick one story: Krishna and the hill, or Ganesha and the race. Draw the most important part. Tell a grown-up what happens and what families say it teaches.
tips: Tell what happens first, next and last.
Say "Families say..." when you tell the lesson.
Use a word from this unit, like share or obstacle.

title: Krishna, Ganesha and the Stories Families Tell

chapters.title: Krishna and the Mountain
chapters.bigQuestion: How can we share and keep others safe?

story.title: A Hill Like an Umbrella
story.kicker: Rain pours for days, and a boy holds up a whole hill on one finger.
paragraphs: Rain falls on the little village. It falls and falls. The cows moo. The children shiver. Water fills the paths between the houses.
A cowherd boy looks at the big hill nearby. His name is Krishna. "Come with me," he tells everyone. "I will keep you safe."
Krishna lifts the whole hill! He holds it up on one small finger. It is like a giant umbrella. People and cows crowd under it, warm and dry.
Many Hindus love this story. They tell it to their children again and again. It is one of many stories about Krishna as a boy.
story.think: Krishna kept everyone safe. Who keeps you safe when it storms?

lessons.title: A Boy in a Cowherd Village
lessons.mainIdea: Krishna grows up in a village of cowherds.
reading: *Krishna* grows up in a small village. The people there care for cows. They are called cowherds.
His mother is Yashoda. She loves him very much. Many Hindus honor Krishna as a form of God. They love the stories of his childhood.

words.d: a cowherd boy in the stories, honored by many Hindus as a form of God
a person who takes care of cows

look.title: Morning in the Village
look.text: Look at the village in the morning. Cows walk to the green fields. Children run beside them. A little blue boy plays a flute. The cows turn to listen.
look.prompt: What sounds might you hear in this village?

check.why: The stories say Krishna grew up in a village of cowherds.

check.q: Who is Krishna's mother in these stories?
check.why: Yashoda raises Krishna in the village.
A cowherd takes care of cows.

lessons.title: The Butter Pot
lessons.mainIdea: Little Krishna loves butter, and families smile at his tricks.
reading: Yashoda makes fresh butter. She keeps it in a clay pot. Little Krishna loves butter. He sneaks some from the pot!
His friends help him reach it. Yashoda finds butter on his face. She is cross, but she loves him. Families smile at this story.

words.d: a soft, rich food made from milk

look.title: The Boy Who Loved Butter
look.text: Little Krishna takes butter from the pots and shares it with his friends and even the monkeys. Yashoda tries to catch him.
look.cite: Retold from the Bhagavata Purana, Book 10, chapters 8 and 9
look.prompt: Krishna shares the butter. Who does he share it with?

check.q: What does little Krishna love to eat?
check.why: The stories say little Krishna loves butter.

check.q: Where does Yashoda keep the butter?
check.why: Yashoda keeps the butter in a clay pot.

check.q: How does Yashoda feel about Krishna?
check.why: Yashoda is cross, but she loves Krishna very much.

lessons.title: Sharing With Friends
lessons.mainIdea: Krishna shares what he has with his friends.
reading: Krishna does not keep the butter all to himself. He shares it with his friends. Everyone gets a taste.
Many families tell this part on purpose. It helps children think about sharing. Sharing makes friends happy.

words.d: to give some of what you have to others

look.title: One Snack, Many Friends
look.text: Look at the boy with a bowl of butter. Four friends sit near him. He gives each friend a scoop. They all laugh together.
look.prompt: Tell about a time you shared something. How did it feel?

check.q: What does Krishna do with the butter?
check.why: In the stories, Krishna shares the butter with his friends.
To share is to give some of what you have to others.

check.q: Why do families tell the sharing part?
choices: To help children think about sharing
check.why: Families use the story to talk about sharing.

lessons.title: Rain and Wind
lessons.mainIdea: A huge storm comes to Krishna's village.
reading: One day dark clouds come. Rain pours down. The wind blows hard. It rains for days and days.
The story says Indra, king of the sky, sent the storm. The people and cows are cold and afraid. They need a safe place.

words.d: strong wind and heavy rain

look.title: Stormy Sky
look.text: Look at the gray sky. Rain comes down like long strings. Trees bend in the wind. A calf hides behind its mother.
look.prompt: What do you do to stay safe in a storm?

check.why: A huge storm comes to the village.

check.q: Who does the story say sent the storm?
check.why: The story says Indra sent the storm.
The people and cows are cold and afraid in the storm.

lessons.title: Lifting Govardhan Hill
lessons.mainIdea: Krishna lifts Govardhan Hill to keep everyone safe.
reading: Krishna walks to Govardhan Hill. He lifts it up with one hand. He holds it on one finger!
Everyone runs under the hill. The cows come too. They stay dry for seven days. Then the storm stops.

words.d: the hill Krishna lifts in the story

look.title: Seven Days Under the Hill
look.text: Krishna holds up the hill for seven days. The people and cows rest under it. When the rain stops, they all come out safe.
look.cite: Retold from the Bhagavata Purana, Book 10, chapter 25
look.prompt: How long does Krishna hold up the hill?

check.why: Krishna lifts Govardhan Hill in the story.
The hill keeps the rain off like a giant umbrella.

check.q: How long do they stay under the hill?
check.why: The Bhagavata Purana says Krishna held the hill for seven days.

lessons.title: Janmashtami
lessons.mainIdea: Many Hindus celebrate Krishna's birthday at Janmashtami.
reading: Janmashtami is Krishna's birthday festival. It comes in late summer. Many Hindu families celebrate it.
Some families stay up until midnight. The stories say Krishna was born at midnight. Some rock a little cradle. They sing songs about baby Krishna.

words.d: the festival for Krishna's birthday

look.title: A Tiny Cradle
look.text: Look at the home shrine. A tiny cradle has flowers all around it. A family sings softly. A clock shows it is almost midnight.
look.prompt: Why do you think the family waits until midnight?

check.why: Janmashtami celebrates Krishna's birthday.

check.q: When do the stories say Krishna was born?
check.why: The stories say Krishna was born at midnight.
Some families rock a little cradle for baby Krishna.

lessons.title: Stories at Home
lessons.mainIdea: Families tell Krishna stories to share what they value.
reading: Families tell Krishna stories at Janmashtami. They tell about the butter. They tell about the hill.
The stories help children talk about big ideas. Share with others. Keep others safe. Hindu families in Illinois tell them too.

words.d: a special day or days when people celebrate together

look.title: Krishna Stories in This Chapter
look.prompt: How many Krishna stories did you learn?

check.q: When do families tell Krishna stories?
check.why: Many families tell Krishna stories at Janmashtami.

check.q: Which big idea goes with the hill story?
check.why: Krishna lifts the hill to keep everyone safe.

check.q: Which big idea goes with the butter story?
check.why: Krishna shares the butter with his friends.

review.q: Who is Krishna's mother in the stories?
What does little Krishna sneak from the pot?
Why does Krishna lift the hill?
choices: To keep people safe from the storm
review.why: He holds it up like an umbrella in the storm.

review.q: How do many Hindus honor Krishna?
review.why: Many Hindus honor Krishna as a form of God.

chapters.title: Ganesha and the Race Around the World
chapters.bigQuestion: How can thinking in a new way help us?

story.title: The Race in the Garden
story.kicker: Two brothers race around the whole world, and one of them never leaves the garden.
paragraphs: Two brothers sit in a garden. One is Kartikeya. The other is Ganesha. Their parents are Shiva and Parvati. "Let's have a race," says their father.
"Go around the whole world," he says. "The first one back wins." Kartikeya jumps on his peacock. Whoosh! He flies away fast.
Ganesha rides a little mouse. The mouse is slow. Ganesha thinks and thinks. Then he stands up and walks around his mother and father.
"You are my whole world," Ganesha says. His parents smile. Ganesha wins the race. He never even left the garden! His brother is still flying.
story.think: Ganesha found a new way to win. Why did his parents like his answer?

lessons.title: The Elephant-Headed One
lessons.mainIdea: Ganesha has an elephant head, and many Hindus honor him.
reading: *Ganesha* has the head of an elephant. He has a big round belly. He often holds a sweet in one hand.
Many Hindus honor Ganesha. They love him very much. His parents are Shiva and Parvati. Hindus honor them too.

words.d: a deity with an elephant head, honored by many Hindus as the remover of obstacles

look.title: Ganesha in the Hall
look.text: Look at the murti by the front door. A murti is a sacred image. This one is Ganesha. He has big ears and a curled trunk. A small mouse sits at his feet.
look.prompt: What do you notice first about Ganesha?

check.q: What kind of head does Ganesha have?
check.why: Ganesha has the head of an elephant.
The stories say Ganesha's parents are Shiva and Parvati.
Hindus call a sacred image a murti.

lessons.title: Remover of Obstacles
lessons.mainIdea: Many Hindus pray to Ganesha before new beginnings.
reading: An obstacle is something in your way. Many Hindus call Ganesha the remover of obstacles.
So many Hindus pray to Ganesha before something new. It might be a new school year or a new home. It might be a trip.

words.d: something that is in your way
a name many Hindus give Ganesha

look.title: A New Beginning
look.text: Look at the family in their new home. Boxes are still on the floor. First, they set a small Ganesha murti on a shelf. They light a lamp near it.
look.prompt: Why might this family think of Ganesha first in a new home?

check.why: An obstacle is something that blocks your way.

check.q: What do many Hindus call Ganesha?
check.why: Many Hindus call Ganesha the remover of obstacles.

check.q: When do many Hindus pray to Ganesha?
check.why: Many Hindus pray to Ganesha before new beginnings.

lessons.title: Ganesha's Mouse
reading: Ganesha is big. But he rides a tiny mouse! The mouse is his helper. It goes everywhere with him.
Artists often paint the mouse at his feet. Some say the mouse shows that small things matter too.

words.d: a small animal; Ganesha's helper in the stories

look.title: Big and Small
look.text: Look at the painting. Ganesha is big and smiling. The mouse is very small. It looks up at Ganesha. It holds a sweet in its paws.
look.prompt: Why do you think a big Ganesha rides a small mouse?

check.why: In the stories, Ganesha rides a little mouse.

check.q: Where do artists often paint the mouse?
check.why: The mouse often sits at Ganesha's feet in pictures.

check.q: What do some say the mouse shows?
check.why: Some say the little mouse shows that small things matter.

lessons.title: Two Brothers
lessons.mainIdea: Ganesha and Kartikeya race around the world.
reading: Ganesha has a brother named Kartikeya. Kartikeya rides a fast peacock. Their parents give them a race.
"Go around the whole world," they say. Kartikeya flies off at once. Ganesha's mouse is slow. What can he do?

words.d: Ganesha's brother, who rides a peacock

look.title: Fast and Slow
look.text: Look at the two brothers. Kartikeya sits on a peacock. Its bright tail feathers spread wide. Ganesha sits on a little mouse. The mouse takes tiny steps.
look.prompt: Who do you think will be faster? Why?

check.why: Kartikeya is Ganesha's brother.
Kartikeya rides a fast peacock.
The brothers race around the whole world.

lessons.title: My Parents Are My World
lessons.mainIdea: Ganesha walks around his parents and says they are his world.
reading: Ganesha thinks hard. Then he walks slowly around his mother and father. He goes all the way around them.
"You are my world," he says. His parents are happy. They say Ganesha wins. He thought in a new way.

words.d: to show great respect and love

look.title: Ganesha's Answer
look.text: Ganesha walks around his parents. He says that going around them is like going around the whole world. His parents agree he has won.
look.cite: Retold from the Shiva Purana, Rudra Samhita, Kumara Khanda, and from family tellings
look.prompt: What does Ganesha mean when he says his parents are his world?

check.why: Ganesha walks around his parents, Shiva and Parvati.
Ganesha says his parents are his world.
His parents say Ganesha wins.

lessons.title: Ganesha's Festival
lessons.mainIdea: Many Hindus celebrate Ganesha at Ganesh Chaturthi.
reading: Ganesh Chaturthi is Ganesha's festival. It comes in late summer. Many Hindu families bring home a Ganesha murti.
They offer flowers and sweets. They sing songs. Many cities have big parades. Families in Illinois celebrate it too.

words.d: a festival that honors Ganesha

look.title: Sweets for Ganesha
look.text: Look at the plate. It has round sweets called modak. Many families say Ganesha loves modak. A child sets the plate near the murti with care.
look.prompt: Why do families set out foods they say Ganesha loves?

check.why: Ganesh Chaturthi honors Ganesha.
Families offer flowers and sweets.

check.q: What sweet do many say Ganesha loves?
check.why: Many families say Ganesha loves modak.

lessons.title: Thinking in a New Way
lessons.mainIdea: Ganesha's story helps children think about new ideas and honoring parents.
reading: Kartikeya was fast. Ganesha was clever. He found a new way to solve the problem.
Families tell this story to talk about two things. Think in a new way. Honor the people who care for you.

words.d: good at thinking of smart ideas

look.title: A Tricky Problem
look.text: Look at the girl at the table. Her puzzle piece does not fit. She stops. She turns the piece around. Click! Now it fits.
look.prompt: How is the girl like Ganesha in the race?

choices: He thought in a new way
check.why: Ganesha was clever and found a new way.

choices: Good at thinking of smart ideas
check.why: Clever means good at thinking of smart ideas.

check.q: What else does the story teach?
choices: Honor the people who care for you
check.why: Ganesha honors his parents in the story.

What do many Hindus call Ganesha?
review.why: Many Hindus call Ganesha the remover of obstacles.

review.q: What does Kartikeya ride in the race?
What does Ganesha do to win?
review.why: Ganesha walks around his parents and says they are his world.
